name: Gibraltar
summary_text: Gibraltar is a self-governing British Overseas Territory with its own Parliament and its own Supreme Court, which between them make and interpret its civil and criminal law. Measures enacted by the United Kingdom do not apply here of their own force: the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued in 2025 bind Gibraltar only if extended by Order in Council, and no such extension appears in the sourced material.  The principal legal gap facing a trans visitor is gender recognition. No process exists in Gibraltar for changing a legal gender marker, and the sourced material records that transgender persons are not permitted to change legal gender. A trans visitor therefore travels on a document whose marker cannot be altered by any local route, and can expect to be read at the border and in public under that marker.  Statutory discrimination protection covering gender reassignment, alongside sexual orientation, has been in place since 2007 under Gibraltar's own equality provisions.  Hate-crime coverage now extends to trans people. Parliament amended the Crimes Act in September 2013 to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, with royal assent on 25 September and effect from 10 October 2013, and in July 2026 passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for transgender identity.  In July 2026 Parliament also passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practise conversion therapy.  Partner and family recognition is established locally: civil partnerships since 2014, same-sex marriage since December 2016 after a bill passed unanimously, a Supreme Court ruling of 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, and an Adoption Act 2023 in full effect from 18 April 2024 that expressly allows same-sex couples to adopt without discrimination.  The age of consent for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender is 16. The Supreme Court ruled on 8 April 2011 that the previous age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set the equal age of 16 with effect from 23 November 2012.  The House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee's 2008 inquiry into overseas territories recommended that discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status be made illegal in all overseas territories, and its Seventh Report of 2007-08 sets accountability and good-governance expectations applicable to Gibraltar.

name: French Guiana
summary_text: French Guiana is an overseas department of France and stands under the French national framework. Identity documents, the criminal code, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime operate there exactly as in metropolitan France, and there is no separate local legislation on gender identity.  Legal gender recognition has been available on a simplified administrative basis since 2017, by declaration before a civil-status officer, with no requirement of surgery, sterilisation or psychiatric diagnosis. Anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity has been in force since 2012, and hate-crime sentence enhancement provisions were added in 2017. Nothing in French law criminalises trans status or gender expression.  Same-sex relations and same-sex marriage are legal under French law, and Pride events are held in the territory. The visible scene is small and anchored in Cayenne, with no venues listed by the GayOut travel guide, which rates French Guiana "Very Safe for LGBTQ+". That rating rests on formal legality rather than on the detention and healthcare conditions described below.  The most serious documented risk is custodial. A BuzzFeed News feature of January 2018 found that trans women incarcerated in France on the basis of their legal gender occupy a legal gray area, with placement decided case by case and little consistent protection; that practice governs the prisons of French Guiana. The CGLPL, the national body responsible for places of deprivation of liberty, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding that serious violations in the treatment of transgender detainees persist across French places of detention, a finding that extends to the territory.  Access to specialised transgender healthcare is limited by distance from mainland treatment centres, which adds travel cost and delay to any medical step in transition. Socially, transphobia and cultural taboos discourage visibility and make reporting of abuse less likely, including reporting to police.

sources.title: French Penal Code Article 225-1 as amended 18 November 2016
sources.documents: Prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity; applicable in French Guiana as overseas department of France.
sources.detail: Cited in text as article 225-1 amended to replace 'sexual identity' with 'gender identity' on 18 November 2016; prior protections enacted 1985 (sexual orientation) and July 2012 (sexual identity). No URL visible in provided text.
